A durable workflow then validates the client, checks policy and benefit eligibility, pauses for analyst review when
required, and creates one idempotent payment request after approval. The Payment System confirms the result
through a signed callback. A reconciler checks payments that remain pending or have an uncertain network result.
The production design uses API Gateway, ECS Fargate, Step Functions, EventBridge, SQS and Aurora PostgreSQL. The
case study code stays smaller: a modular Spring Boot application, three external-system stubs, Docker Compose,
and ports that can later be connected to AWS services.
Once the intake API has accepted a claim, the claim must not disappear. A temporary failure may slow the
process down, but it must not create a duplicate claim, a duplicate payment or an unclear status.

1.1 What the current picture tells me
The Claims UI and API currently sit in the middle of the process, but the surrounding systems are not connected. The
Channel System can produce JSON, the Client Registry owns client information, the Policy Manager owns policy and
benefit rules, and the third-party Payment System executes payments.
The new solution therefore needs to connect the process without taking ownership away from those systems. The
Claims Platform may store the evidence returned by an external system, but it should not become the master source
for client, policy or settlement data.

When a claim needs review, the workflow creates a work item and waits for a callback token. The token is mapped to
the claim, not shown in the browser, and completed only through an authorised API. The analyst sees the client and
policy results, records a reasoned decision, and the workflow continues from the same point.
A temporary technical failure is not a business rejection. The workflow records the failed step, retries only when it is
safe, and raises an operational alert when the retry limit is reached. The claim stays in a clear state such as
with a technical sub-status, rather than being rejected by mistake.

8.2 Why there is no distributed transaction
A single transaction cannot safely span Aurora, Client Registry, Policy Manager and a third-party payment provider. I
use local transactions, explicit state, idempotent commands and reconciliation instead.
An optimistic lock version protects the claim row. If two updates race, one update receives a conflict, reloads the
claim and re-checks whether the requested transition is still valid. Database unique constraints remain the final
protection for duplicate submissions and processed events.

20. Delivery plan, AI use and conclusion
I used AI as a review and drafting assistant. It helped me challenge failure scenarios, compare architecture options
and improve parts of the document. I reviewed the design, rewrote the final explanation in my own words, checked
the code and kept responsibility for the technical decisions. I would be able to explain or change every part of the
The proposed platform connects the existing systems without weakening their ownership. It accepts claims safely,
coordinates client and policy checks, supports analyst decisions, creates payment requests only after approval and
keeps one clear audit trail from submission to settlement.
The most important part of the design is not the number of AWS services. It is the way failures are handled: an
accepted claim is durable, duplicate work is safe, uncertain payments are reconciled, urgent claims receive capacity,
and operations can see what is happening.
A temporary downstream failure may delay a claim, but it must never lose an accepted claim, create a
duplicate payment, or leave the business unable to explain what happened.
